class extremum_seeking.averaging.PerturbationDerivativeEstimation(n, p, T, t, zero_mean=True)¶

Bases: object

Handles the calculations of perturbation signals and estimators.

For extremum seeking, one is concerned with finding the derivatives of the cost function \(J:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) in a model-free way. The derivatives up to the \(m\) -th order can be estimated around an estimate of the optimal parameter \(\hat{\theta}\) using a time-varying perturbed cost function output and a time-varying estimation signal as in

\[\hat{\xi}(\omega t, \hat{\theta}, a) = h(\omega t, a)\cdot J( \hat{\theta} + a\cdot p(\omega t))\]

where \(\hat{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^o\) is an estimate of the various derivatives of \(J\) at \(\hat{\theta}\) stored in a vector \(\xi\), \(p:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a periodic (for this package) perturbation signal scaled by a small parameter \(a\) and speed up by a large parameter \(\omega\), and \(h:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^o\) is the signal used to estimate the derivatives from the output. Note that we do not expect that \(\hat{\xi}\) to be close to the derivatives of \(J\) but rather the averaged estimate

\[\hat{\bar{\xi}}(\hat{\bar{\theta}}, a) = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^T \hat{\xi}(\tau, \hat{\bar{\theta}}, a) d\tau\]

converges to the true derivative vector as \(a\to 0\). To accomplish this, we construct \(h\) based on an order \(m\) polynomial cost function, which in multiindex notation, is

\[J(\theta - \hat{\theta}) = \sum_{\vert \alpha \vert \leq m} \frac{1}{\alpha!} D^{\alpha}J(\hat{\theta}) (\theta - \hat{\theta})^{\alpha}\]

with \(\alpha\) being a multiindex and \(D^{\alpha}\) being a short hand for the derivative \(\left(\frac{\partial} {\partial\theta_1}\right)^{\alpha_1}\cdots\left(\frac{\partial} {\partial\theta_1}\right)^{\alpha_n}\) . For simplicity, we can rearrange this summation into a linear algebra problem with

\[J(\hat{\theta} + a\cdot p(\tau)) = J(\hat{\theta}) + \rho(\tau)^T A \xi(\hat{\theta})\]

with \(\rho(\tau)\) being a vector to track all the \(p(\tau)^{\alpha}\) and \(A\) is a diagonal matrix that accounts for \(a^{\vert \alpha \vert}/\alpha!\) for all derivatives with an order of at least 1. We call \(\rho\) the extended perturbation signal, \(\bar{\rho}\) is average value, and \(\tilde{\rho}\) is deviation from the mean. The crux of knowing if an \(h\) exists is if one must show that \(\tilde{\rho}\) is a vector of linearly independent signals which is equivalent to the check of the covariance matrix

\[Q := \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^\tau \tilde{\rho}(\tau) \tilde{\rho}(\tau)^T d\tau\]

being a positive definite matrix. One solution for \(h\) is with the covariance matrix as

\[h_Q(\tau, a) = A^{-1} Q^{-1} \tilde{\rho}(\tau)\]

although the solution is nonunique. If one had another vector of zero-mean signals \(r:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^o\) , the crossvariance

\[R := \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^\tau r(\tau) \tilde{\rho}(\tau)^T d\tau\]

is used to construct the solution

\[h_R(\tau, a) = A^{-1} R^{-1} r(\tau)\]

For historical reasons, it possible to use signals that are not zero-mean. This can be included by setting the zero_mean keyword argument to False when intializing the class object. In this case, we do keep track of all vectors and matrices but this time with the 0th order derivative as well.

calculate_coefficient_matrix(m, scaling_factor=None)¶

Calculates the coefficient matrix \(A\) .

The coefficient matrix \(A\) is a diagonal matrix with the diagonal elements \(A_{ii} = a^{\vert \alpha_i \vert} / \alpha_{i}!\) corresponding to the \(i\) -th element of the ordered multiindex set \(\mathcal{A}\) .

Parameters

  • m (int) – order of the estimation.

  • scaling_factor (Sympy.Expr or None) – Factor for scaling based on the perturbation input scalaing. Defaults to \(a\) .

calculate_covariance_matrix(m)¶

Calculates the covariance matrix of the perturbation signals.

Function to calculate the covariance matrix \(Q\) and determines whether the matrix is invertible. If it is invertible then the demodulation signal \(h(t,a)\) signal exists.

Parameters

m – maximum order of derivatives being considered.

Returns

the covariance matrix of the extended

perturbations as a square sympy.Matrix .

is_invertible: boolean value of whether the \(Q\) is invertible

Return type

covariance_matrix

calculate_crossvariance_matrix(m, r)¶

Generate the crossvariance \(R\) based on the users input choice of periodic signals. They should have a common period with the perturbations \(p\) .

Parameters

  • m – maximum order of derivatives being considered.

  • r – list of m zero-mean signals for derivative estimation

Returns

the crossvariance matrix between signals is_invertible: boolean on if \(R\) is invertible.

R

calculate_extended_perturbation_averages(m)¶

Determines the average value of the extended perturbations.

The average extended perturbations as defined as

\[\bar{\rho} = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T} \rho(\tau) d\tau\]
Parameters

m (int) – the maximum order of the derivatives being considered.

Returns

the averages of the extended perturbation signal vector up to order \(m\) .

calculate_extended_perturbation_deviations(m)¶

Calculates the deviation of the extended perturbation from the average as \(\tilde{\rho}(\tau) = \rho(\tau) - \bar{\rho}\) .

Parameters

m – is the maximum order of the derivatives being estimated.

Returns

Deviation of extended perturbation signal vector from the average.

calculate_extended_perturbations(m)¶

Calculates the extended perturbation vector up to order m.

The extended perturbation is defined as a vector with the elements

\[\rho(\tau)_i = p(\tau)^{\alpha_i},\ i=1,2,\ldots \vert \mathcal{A} \vert\]

for the ordered set of \(\mathcal{A}\) , which contains all the multiindices of interest.

Parameters

m (int) – maximum derivative order to calculate

Returns

A sympy vector of the extended perturbations.

derivative_order()¶

Gives the derivative order of each multiindex i.e. \(\vert \alpha \vert\) for every multiindex being tracked.

property m_max¶

Maximum derivative order of the multiindex set which was calculated. The current multiindex set \(\mathcal{A}\) will satisfy \(\vert \alpha \vert \leq m_{\max}\) for all \(\alpha\in \mathcal{A}\) .

multiindex_factorial()¶

Returns the multiindex factorial \(\alpha!\) for all multiindices being tracked.

property multiindex_set¶

The ordered set of multiindices of the derivatives.

This property is the ordered set \(\mathcal{A}\) which contains the all the multiindices \(\alpha\) in a numpy.ndarray . The ordering is so that the \(i\) -th and \(j\) -th elements of \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfy \(\vert \alpha_i \vert \leq \alpha_j \vert\) for all \(i< j\) . The first index represents the order and the second represents the individual elements of \(\alpha_i\).

property perturbations¶

List of base perturbation signals \(p\) .

class extremum_seeking.filters.DirectionalFilter(g)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.filters.base_filters.Filter

Filter that outputs a direction rather than derivative.

Simple wrapper class to allow for a ParameterUpdateODE to become a filter. The main reason behind this is that the parameter systems update the parameters based on a direction that “should” improve the cost function. For vehicles with kinematic constraints, we could like to know this direction and then attempt to move along this direction.

class extremum_seeking.filters.LowPassRicattiFilter(omega_l, ndim)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.filters.base_filters.Filter

Low Pass Ricatti Based Inverse Filter for Matrices

Used for the low pass filter of a symmetric inverse matrix. Let \(Y \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^{n\times n}\) be a positive definite symmetric matrix estimated by a low pass filter version \(X\). If \(XZ = I\), then

\[\frac{d}{dt} Z = \omega_{l} \left(Z - ZYZ \right)\]

This matrix differential transformed into a vector differential equation by using a Kronecker product.

\[\frac{d}{dt} \text{vec}(Z) = \omega_{l} \left(\text{vec}(Z) - (Z \otimes Z) \text{vec}(Y)\right)\]

class extremum_seeking.seekers.AcceleratedGradientFlow(k, r=3.0, t0=0.01)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.seekers.parameter_odes.ParameterUpdateODE

Accelerated Gradient Methods

\[\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\hat{\theta} + \frac{r}{t + t_0} \frac{d}{dt}\hat{\theta} + k\nabla J = 0\]

This computationally calculated using the system of equations

\[\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt} \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\theta} \\ \frac{d}{dt}\hat{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{d}{dt}\hat{\theta} \\ -\frac{r}{t + t_0} \left(\frac{d}{dt}\hat{\theta}\right) - k \nabla J \end{bmatrix}\end{split}\]
Method Types:

  • Accelerated Gradient Method (AGM): \(r \in [0,\infty),\ t_0 > 0\)

  • Optimized Gradient Method Gradient based (OGM-G):

    \(r = -3,\ t_0 = -T < 0\)

class extremum_seeking.seekers.DirectExtremumSeeker(g, h, J, p)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.seekers.simulators.Seeker, extremum_seeking.seekers.simulators.ParameterizedSystem

Direct Extremum Seeker – Acts directly on the source field or map.

A Direct Extremum Eeeker operates directly on the cost function/source field/map. This is analogous to an Extremum Seeker with fast state dynamics or a continous time perturbation based optimizer. This block diagram is as follows:

                                        Cost Function
                  \theta(t)           +--------------+
   +----------------------------------+ J(t, \theta) |---+-----> y(t)
   |                                  +--------------+   |
   |                                                     |
   |                                                     |
   |                                                     V
+--+---+                            Derivative  +--------+-----------+
| p(t) | Perturbation               Estimation  | \dot{z} = h(t,z,y) +
+--+---+                                        +--------+-----------+
   ^                                                     |
   |                                                     | z(t)
   | \hat{\theta}                                        |
   |                                                     |
   |             Parameter Estimate Dynamics             |
   |      +-----------------------------------------+    |
   +------+ \dot{\hat{\theta} = g(t,\hat{\theta},z) +<---+
          +-----------------------------------------+

class extremum_seeking.seekers.LieBracketSeeker(f, h, J, u)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.seekers.simulators.Seeker, extremum_seeking.seekers.simulators.DynamicalSystem

Extremum Seeker using Lie Brackets

Extremum seeking where the controller directly takes in derivative estimates to modify the controller. The block diagram appears like

                                             Cost
         System Dynamics                   Function
   +-------------------------------+ x(t) +---------+
+->+ \dot{x} = f(t, x, u(t, x; z)) +----->+ J(t, x) |--+-----> y(t)
|  +-------------------------------+      +---------+  |
|                                                      |
|                                                      |
|              Estimation Filters                      |
|     z(t)  +---------------------+                    |
+-----------+ \dot{z} = h(t,z,y)  +--------------------+
            +---------------------+

and the state ODE can be rewritten into the special affine form of

\[\dot{x} = f_{0}(t, x) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} f_{i}(t,x) \omega^{p_i} u'_{i}(k_i\omega t)\]

where \(p\in (0,1)\), \(k_i \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}\), and \(u'_{i}\) is a \(2\pi\) periodic function.

class extremum_seeking.seekers.NewtonFlow(k, omega_l, odim)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.seekers.parameter_odes.ParameterUpdateODE

Newton Flow

Spatial second order method involving the Hessian of the cost function. Updates the estimate of the optimal parameters \(\hat{\theta}\) using the gradient \(\nabla J\) and an estimate of the inverse Hessian \(\hat{\Gamma}\). To achieve this we use the following differential equations

where scalars \(k\) and \(\omega_{l}\) are the gain and filter rate. We are estimating the inverse Hessian based on the low pass inverse Ricatti equation.

class extremum_seeking.systems.PursuerEvaderGame(f_pursuer, f_evader)¶

Bases: extremum_seeking.systems.System

System of a two player pursuer-evader game.

This class is to simulate a pursuer-evader game. The game assumes two players, each with their own, independent dynamics.

\[\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt} x_{p} &= f(t, x_{p}, u_{p}) \\ \frac{d}{dt} x_{e} &= f(t, x_{e}, u_{e})\end{split}\]

where: * \(x_{p}\) is the pursuer states. * \(x_{e}\) is the evader states. * \(u_{p}\) is the pursuer controller vector. * \(u_{e}\) is the evader controller vector.

Note that one expects that the controllers will have feedback on both player states. The call signatures of the respective controllers look like

\[u_{i}(t, x_{p}, x_{e}, theta)\]
